name: fake
intent: Replace a depended-on component with a much lighter-weight but genuinely working implementation - usually backed by in-memory data structures - so tests exercise real interaction sequences without the latency, side effects and availability problems of the real component.
problem: Tests that use the real depended-on component are slow (disk or network round trips), unavailable or expensive to provision in the development environment, and leave side effects behind; but the system under test interacts with that component as a real sequence - values written by one call are read back by later calls - which canned stub answers and expectation-based mocks cannot express faithfully.
context: Unit and component tests around a system under test whose collaborator is infrastructure or an external system (database, repository, web service, service layer, message broker, file system, clock) where a substitutable dependency exists or can be extracted and the subset of the collaborator's contract that the system under test exercises can be implemented cheaply and correctly in memory.
benefits: Order-of-magnitude faster tests: keeping the store in memory removes the dominant cost of disk and network I/O, which is why Meszaros' team ran a suite roughly 50 times faster after faking out the database with hash tables.

The tests stop encoding the collaborator's call sequence: the system under test may call the fake as often and in whatever order it needs, so refactorings no longer fail tests that were only pinning down interaction order (Meszaros' Overspecified Software smell).
No per-test configuration ceremony: the fake works out of the box, so a test reads as the behaviour of the system under test instead of as setup code for a double.
One lightweight implementation is shared by many tests, unlike a purpose-built stub per scenario, and it grows only as tests demand more services.

Tests keep exercising realistic sequences - write then read, publish then subscribe - instead of pre-programmed answers, so the interaction with the collaborator still exercises the system under test's real logic.
Tests run when the real component is unavailable, licensed, rate-limited or side-effecting in the development environment.
tradeoffs: Fake and reality drift: the fake is a second implementation of the same contract, so when the real component's behaviour changes (constraints, transactions, ordering, error semantics) the suite stays green while production breaks.

A self-consistent fake can still be wrong in ways the tests cannot see: a hash-table store accepts duplicates, ignores transaction rollback or lacks the real component's failure modes, so tests pass for behaviour the real system cannot exhibit.

Fidelity costs maintenance: as more tests use it the fake grows towards a re-implementation of the real component with its own bug surface, and Meszaros' precondition - building the fake must stay easier than building the mocks - eventually stops holding.
Stateful fakes invite hidden test-order coupling: writes persist across tests unless the fixture re-creates or clears the store, which turns an unrelated later test into the failure.

It is no substitute for integration or contract testing: the fake proves nothing about the real adapter (SQL dialect, wire format, authentication), so at least one test against the real collaborator remains mandatory.
Interaction assertions are unavailable by design: a fake records nothing and expects nothing, so when the interaction sequence itself is the behaviour under test a mock or spy must be used instead.
Installing the fake requires a substitutable dependency in production code - an extracted interface, an injection point or a registry - which is a design change made for testability alone.

participants.responsibility: Test-only implementation of the depended-on component's services that really works but takes a shortcut (in-memory store, no concurrency, no durability); it is not configured with expectations or canned answers.
The abstraction (interface, protocol, trait, port) through which the system under test calls the collaborator; the fake implements the same services so the substitution is invisible.
The code being tested, which calls the fake through the production interface and is unaware that it is not talking to the real component.

The seam through which the fake is installed - constructor or parameter injection, factory, registry, or a test-specific subclass hook - chosen to match how the system under test resolves its collaborators.
Optional test-only route (Data Loader, Back Door Setup) that puts fixture state directly into the fake instead of driving the real component's API, avoiding data sensitivity and overspecification.
Kept in the suite by at least one integration or contract test, so divergence between the fake's behaviour and the real implementation is detected.

use_cases: Replacing a database or persistence layer with in-memory hash tables so the suite stops paying disk latency (Meszaros' motivating example, and the origin of the In-Memory Database variation).
A hand-written in-memory implementation of a repository or gateway port that many tests share, where writes made by the system under test must be visible to its later reads.
Standing in for an external web service or a service layer with a small hard-coded or data-driven implementation so tests are robust and need no test instance of the remote system.
Running the whole application against a lightweight subsystem in a demo or local development environment - an embedded database, an in-process broker - where the real component cannot be provisioned.

Using a ready-made in-memory subsystem that already implements the contract more faithfully than a hand-rolled map: an embedded database (SQLite in-memory, H2), an in-memory file system (Go's testing/fstest.MapFS) or an in-process HTTP test server.
A fake clock or identifier generator that really advances and produces values, so time- and id-dependent logic is exercised deterministically without canned per-call answers.
Testing code that accesses a remote service where a Self-Initializing Fake (Fowler) first records real responses and then replays them, reducing network dependence while maintaining realistic data.
Faking a message broker or event bus with an in-memory queue so publish-subscribe interactions are tested without infrastructure dependencies.

The Kubernetes client-go library ships a generated fake clientset (k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/fake) whose in-memory ObjectTracker really processes create/update/delete/watch, so controllers and reconcile loops are unit-tested without an API server.

Moto (getmoto/moto) keeps in-memory state behind fake implementations of the AWS APIs (S3, EC2, DynamoDB) so boto3-based code runs its real interaction sequences without ever reaching an AWS endpoint.

Ready-made fake transports and clocks: Rails' ActionMailer :test delivery method appends real Mail objects to the in-memory ActionMailer::Base.deliveries collection, and Guava's FakeTicker (guava-testlib) really advances time by explicit steps instead of returning canned instants.
avoid_when: The test needs canned answers or an assertion about which calls happened: a Test Stub, Test Spy or Mock Object expresses that directly, while a fake deliberately has neither configuration nor expectations.
Only one test needs one fixed response: a hard-coded test double (anonymous implementation, lambda, local function) is simpler than building a working fake.
The real collaborator is fast, deterministic and side-effect free in the test environment: use the real object - it doubles as the test that catches fake/reality drift.

The interaction with the real component is the thing under test (wire format, SQL dialect, transaction semantics, authentication): use a real instance, an embedded/containerised server or consumer-driven contract tests.
The fake would end up larger than the code under test: the abstraction is too wide - extract the decision logic into a plain collaborator that needs no double at all.

The in-memory implementation would be shipped into production to stand in for a missing or degraded service: that is a production resilience decision (fail-safe defaults, graceful degradation), not a test double.
anti_patterns: A 'fake' that returns values configured per test and asserts which calls arrived - that is a Configurable Test Double or Mock Object mislabelled, and it reintroduces the overspecification the fake exists to avoid.
Replacing the very component under test with a fake, so the test verifies the double's behaviour instead of the software's.
Letting the fake grow into a second full implementation of the real component with no drift test, so the suite certifies the fake's semantics rather than the system's contract.
Shipping the fake, or a fake-mode switch, into production code paths so the application can be run with a stub subsystem.
Using an in-memory fake for infrastructure whose behaviour is the contract under test (SQL dialect, transaction isolation, serialization) and treating green unit tests as integration evidence.
Keeping the fake's mutable store in static, module-level or shared-fixture state so writes leak between tests and failures depend on execution order.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: the system under test depends on the collaborator's abstraction, which is what makes a lightweight substitute possible at all.
Separation of concerns: the behaviour under test is isolated from the collaborator's infrastructure concerns - I/O, latency, availability, side effects.
Don't repeat yourself: one reusable working implementation serves many tests instead of a purpose-built double per scenario.
You aren't gonna need it / KISS: the fake implements only the services the current tests exercise and grows incrementally, instead of mirroring the whole interface up front.
Interface segregation: keeping the faked abstraction small is what keeps the fake small and cheap to maintain.
Single responsibility: the fake provides services, not observations - recording interactions or encoding expectations belongs to spy and mock.
best_practices: Implement the fake against exactly the abstraction the system under test consumes (extract an interface first if the collaborator is a concrete class) and install it through the existing substitutable dependency.
Keep the fake self-consistent: anything written through it must be readable back, since that is the behaviour tests rely on.
Start with the subset of services the current tests need and extend the fake only as tests demand, keeping the effort below what building suitable mocks would cost.
Re-create or explicitly clear the fake's store for every test; never keep mutable fake state in static fields, module globals or a shared fixture.
Keep at least one integration or contract test against the real component, so drift between the fake and reality fails loudly.
Do not configure expectations or canned answers on a fake - if the test must control indirect inputs or observe indirect outputs, use a stub, spy or mock instead.
Prefer a ready-made faithful in-memory subsystem (embedded database, in-memory file system, in-process test server) when one exists for the collaborator.
Never let the fake or a fake-selection switch become reachable from production code.
Use the Self-Initializing Fake pattern (Fowler) when testing against a slow or rate-limited remote service: record real responses first, then replay them for repeated test runs.
Ensure the fake's failure modes are at least a superset of the real component's - tests that pass on the fake but fail on the real component indicate a dangerous false sense of security.
sources: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code (Addison-Wesley, 2007) - Fake Object (Test Double Patterns, Chapter 23, p. 551), with variations Fake Database, In-Memory Database, Fake Web Service and Fake Service Layer.

Martin Fowler, Self Initializing Fake (Bliki, 2009) - https://martinfowler.com/bliki/SelfInitializingFake.html - a Fake variant that records from the real service on first run then replays cached responses.
Roy Osherove, The Art of Unit Testing, 3rd ed. (Manning, 2023) - chapters on stubs, mocks, and the role of fakes in breaking dependencies.
Jeff Atwood, Test Doubles: A Taxonomy of Pretend Objects (Coding Horror, 2007) - https://blog.codinghorror.com/test-doubles-a-taxonomy-of-pretend-objects/
Microsoft, Patterns in Practice: Design For Testability (MSDN Magazine, 2008) - demonstrates Repository pattern with in-memory fake implementations for test isolation.

Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns Chapter 23: Test Double Patterns (O'Reilly online edition) - https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/xunit-test-patterns/9780131495050/ch23.html - canonical source of the Fake Object pattern and its In-Memory Database variation.

Kubernetes, k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/fake package documentation - https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/fake - generated fake clientset with an in-memory ObjectTracker used to unit-test controllers without an API server.
Moto - Mock AWS Services - https://github.com/getmoto/moto - in-memory fake implementations of AWS APIs (S3, EC2, DynamoDB) that keep resource state for tests.

Ruby on Rails, ActionMailer::TestHelper API - https://api.rubyonrails.org/v8.1.0/classes/ActionMailer/TestHelper.html - the :test delivery method and in-memory ActionMailer::Base.deliveries collection as a framework-provided mail fake.

Google Guava, FakeTicker (guava-testlib) - https://github.com/google/guava/blob/master/guava-testlib/src/com/google/common/testing/FakeTicker.java - a fake time source that really advances by explicit steps instead of returning canned values.

Philipp Hauer, Don't use In-Memory Databases (H2, Fongo) for Tests - https://phauer.com/2017/dont-use-in-memory-databases-tests-h2/ - the standard critique: in-memory fakes drift from the real engine, so they must not be the only persistence tests.
